title: Natural selection does not inherently drive organisms toward more elaborate structure

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Natural selection does not inherently drive organisms toward more elaborate structure

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Natural selection does not inevitably produce progressively more elaborate organisms; increases in complexity in the fossil record come from random mutations that add features without fatal flaws, while selection's systematic effect is to simplify.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: It is certainly not the case—as is often assumed—that natural selection somehow inevitably leads to organisms with progressively more elaborate structures and progressively larger numbers of parts.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 8, “Implications for Everyday Systems”; section “Fundamental Issues in Biology” (from p. 383), p. 398. Scope: long-term trends in organismal complexity

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch08-18: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.48

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Existing fossil and morphology databases can test whether elaboration is inevitable or monotonic for selected clades and traits. They have weaker power to attribute increases to tolerated mutations or selection-driven simplification. The composite causal claim is therefore only partially resolvable.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Estimate long-term trends in multiple organismal complexity measures from fossil phylogenies and compare trait gains and losses with evidence of selection. A consistent selection-associated increase would refute the no-inherent-drive component, while attributing gains specifically to nonfatal random additions requires mechanistic evidence.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Observed trends do not identify mutation versus selection as their cause.

Complexity has no single accepted measure.

The fossil record strongly biases part counts and preservation.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Public fossil data can reject a claim that organisms inevitably become more elaborate, because many old lineages stay simple and some trends reverse. They do not show that increases come from nonfatal random mutations while selection's systematic effect is to simplify, since those causes are not variables in the occurrence record. The negative half is partly testable; the causal partition is not.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Track a complexity measure, such as number of distinct parts or a disparity statistic, across fossil lineages and test whether the maximum and the typical value rise inevitably, and whether decreases are common. A ceiling that does not rise in many long-lived lineages, together with frequent simplification, would support the negative claim about inevitability; a systematic increase confined to lineages under stronger selection would count against the proposed roles of mutation and selection.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The fossil record shows maximum complexity and typical complexity moving differently, so the trend depends on the statistic.

Random mutation versus selection is not identified by the direction of the trend alone.
